title: Basie as a father figure and introductions in New York
summary: Edison was closest to Freddie Green; Basie took him around New York and introduced him to James P. Johnson, Redman and Ellington.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Who were your big buddies in Basie's band?
Well, Buck was a very close friend to

me. We were all close in that band. Everybody was close in that band. You just couldn't say, well, this is my best buddy. Freddie Green was about my closest friend I had, you know. And Basie is a good buddy to me because I always looked upon him as a father to me.

Yeah. He is responsible for me knowing everybody that I know. Because when I joined the band, he just took a liking to me, you know. And I used to listen to him because I had no fatherly advice when I left home, you know. I just left. Nobody said, 'Now, son, you have to do this, you have to do this, you should do this.' My mother -- they could tell a girl what to do to look out for her, what hazards there were out there.

Yes, yes. So I went to Basie and he just took a liking to me, you know. And he introduced me to James P. Johnson. He introduced me because he was from Red Bank, New Jersey, you see, and he had played in New York in his younger days. He had played all around New York, everybody knew him in New York. And him and Sonny Greer were good buddies, you know. And Kaiser Marshall, all of them knew Basie.

So when I went to New York and when I joined Basie's band, he took me everyplace. He introduced me to Clark Monroe, he introduced me to Don Redman. He introduced me to Duke. He

introduced me to everybody, you know. And what a thrill it was to meet James P. Johnson. And all the people that I had read about and admired, and never had the slightest idea that I would be shaking hands with them. I met them through Basie, you know.

And, I mean, those guys that he introduced me to, they laid a foundation that all piano players still observe today. James P. Johnson with the stride piano, the left-hand rolling and -- oh, let's see. He introduced me to all the dancers at the time, the older dancers. And, you know, I got him -- I'm grateful to him for my whole career.
